'''David Lauri Wiltshire''' is a [[professor]] of [[theoretical physics]] at the [[University of Canterbury]], in [[Christchurch]], New Zealand, where he leads the Gravity and Cosmology Group.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gravity and Cosmology Group |url=https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/research/about-uc-research/research-groups-and-centres/gravity-and-cosmology-group |access-date=2025-01-17 |website=canterbury.ac.nz|date=27 August 2024 }}</ref>

== Career ==
Wiltshire completed undergraduate studies in physics and mathematics and an MSc at the University of Canterbury, Christchurch in 1983.<ref name="dlwbio">{{Cite web |title=David Wiltshire: a short career biography |url=http://www2.phys.canterbury.ac.nz/~dlw24/dlw-bio.html|access-date=2025-01-17 |website=phys.canterbury.ac.nz}}</ref> In 1987, Wiltshire completed a PhD in theoretical physics at [[University of Cambridge]], supervised by [[Gary Gibbons]].<ref name="dlwbio"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=David L Wiltshire - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=96402 |access-date=2024-04-23 |website=mathgenealogy.org}}</ref>

Following his PhD, Wiltshire held [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral]] positions at the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in [[Trieste]], [[Italy]];  the [[University of Newcastle upon Tyne]], [[UK]]; and the [[University of Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], where he then  began lecturing. In July 2001, he returned to the University of Canterbury to take up an academic position in the Department of Physics and Astronomy.<ref name="dlwbio"/>

==Research==

Wiltshire's research interests include [[general relativity]], [[cosmology]] and [[quantum gravity]].

Wiltshire is best known for the [[Inhomogeneous cosmology #Timescape cosmology|timescape cosmology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The dark-energy deniers|url=https://physicsworld.com/a/the-dark-energy-deniers|access-date=2024-09-26|website=physicsworld.com|date=19 June 2018 }}</ref> He reinterprets [[dark energy]] as a misidentification of gradients in [[Mass_in_general_relativity|gravitational energy]] in an inhomogeneous universe, in which the present epoch [[observable universe#Large-scale structure|cosmic web]] is dominated by [[void (astronomy)|voids]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gravitational energy and cosmic "acceleration"
|url=http://www2.phys.canterbury.ac.nz/~dlw24/universe|access-date=2024-09-26 |website=phys.canterbury.ac.nz}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wiltshire |first1=David L. |date=2009 |title=From time to timescape - Einstein's unfinished revolution |journal =Int. J. Mod. Phys. D |volume=18 |issue=14 |pages=2121–2134 |doi=10.1142/S0218271809016193 |arxiv=0912.4563 |bibcode=2009IJMPD..18.2121W }}</ref> His predictions about average cosmic expansion will be subject to precision tests including observations by the [[Euclid_(spacecraft)|Euclid mission]], the [[Dark Energy Survey]], and the [[Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument]] (DESI).

On 19 December 2024, Wiltshire and colleagues announced 
<ref>{{cite web|title=Dark energy 'doesn't exist', so can't be pushing lumpy universe apart -study|date=19 December 2024 |url=https://ras.ac.uk/news-and-press/research-highlights/dark-energy-doesnt-exist-so-cant-be-pushing-lumpy-universe-apart|access-date=2025-01-17}}</ref> the results of a new model-independent statistical analysis of the Pantheon+ [[Supernova#Type I|Type Ia Supernova]] catalogue. They found that the timescape model fit the data better than the standard [[ΛCDM model]] at 99% confidence level, providing evidence for a foundational change to cosmological models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Seifert|first1=Antonia|last2=Lane|first2=Zachary G|last3=Galoppo|first3=Marco|last4=Ridden-Harper|first4=Ryan|last5=Wiltshire|first5=David L| date=2025|title=Supernovae evidence for foundational change to cosmological models |journal=Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc. Lett.|volume=537|issue=1|pages=L55–L60|doi=10.1093/mnrasl/slae112|doi-access=free |arxiv=2412.15143}}</ref>

== Awards ==
In 2023 Wiltshire was awarded the [[Dan Walls]] Medal by the New Zealand Institute of Physics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NZIP Award Recipients – New Zealand Institute of Physics |url=https://nzip.org.nz/about-nzip/nzip-award-recipients/ |access-date=2024-04-23}}</ref>
